summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing IEEE 802.3 repeaters running at 10 and 100 megabits per second, using the SMIv2 format. It lets network management software monitor and control repeater devices.

plainLanguage.summary: An Ethernet repeater is a box that copies electrical signals between ports. This document defines the SNMP objects that let a management system read and change how such a box behaves, and that let it work out which addresses sit behind which port.

questions: how does snmp monitor ethernet repeaters
what changed from rfc 1516 to rfc 2108
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a management system see and control IEEE 802.3 repeaters, in the trees and tables of the MIB.

tldr.problem: A network management system needs a standard way to ask an Ethernet repeater what its ports are doing, to reset it, to see which addresses are attached where, and to read its error counters.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a MIB module, rooted at mib-2 22, whose objects are arranged in four packages: basic status and control, monitoring counters, address tracking, and a Top N report of the busiest ports. It also gives an algorithm for turning the address-to-port information into a map of the physical network.
tldr.outcome: The MIB is a superset of the one in RFC 1516, which it obsoletes, and it adds support for multiple repeaters, 100BASE-T management, port TopN reports, and address search.

today: RFC 2108 is a Proposed Standard from February 1997 that obsoletes RFC 1516. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The SNMP Framework This MIB Belongs To
sections.content:
The SNMP network management framework consists of three major components. The SMI, described in RFC 1902, provides the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. The MIB-II, STD 17, RFC 1213, is the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols. The protocol, STD 15, RFC 1157 and RFC 1905, is used for accessing managed information. Textual conventions are defined in RFC 1903, and conformance statements in RFC 1904. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base. Objects in the MIB are defined using the subset of ASN.1 defined in the SMI. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name, and the object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object. For human convenience a textual string, the descriptor, is often used to refer to the object type.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is one part of the SNMP family: the data model that a management protocol reads. It names each managed object with a number, called an object identifier, so that software can ask for it by name.

sections.title: What the New MIB Adds
sections.content:
The MIB is intended as a superset of the one defined by RFC 1516, which goes to historic status. It includes all of the objects contained in that MIB, plus several new ones providing significant additional capabilities, and implementors are encouraged to support all applicable conformance groups in order to make the best use of the new functionality. The new objects provide support for multiple repeaters, 100BASE-T management, port TopN capability, and address search and topology mapping.

Certain objects have been deprecated. In particular, the scalar objects used for managing a single repeater are now of minimal use, since they are duplicated in the new multiple-repeater definitions, and additional objects have been deprecated based on implementation experience with RFC 1516. The module also carries the objects of the earlier RFC 1368 MIB as a deprecated subtree, and the conformance statement for RFC 1368 is marked obsolete and replaced by one for RFC 1516.
sections.plainLanguage: The new MIB keeps everything the old one had and adds four things: managing several repeaters in one box, managing the 100 Mb/s variant, reporting which ports are busiest, and looking up where an address is attached. The old single-repeater objects are kept but marked as of little use.

sections.title: What the Objects Represent
sections.content:
Instances of the object types defined in the memo represent attributes of an IEEE 802.3 repeater, as defined by Section 9, Repeater Unit for 10 Mb/s Baseband Networks, in the IEEE 802.3/ISO 8802-3 CSMA/CD standard, and Section 27, Repeater for 100 Mb/s Baseband Networks, in IEEE Standard 802.3u-1995. These objects may be used to manage non-standard repeater-like devices, but defining objects to describe implementation-specific properties of such devices is outside the scope of the memo.

The definitions are based on Section 30.4, Layer Management for 10 and 100 Mb/s Baseband Repeaters, and Annex 30A, GDMO Specifications for 802.3 managed objects, of the IEEE document. Implementors should note that the IEEE document explicitly describes when, where and how the various repeater attributes are measured, and also describes the effects of repeater actions that may be invoked by manipulating instances of the MIB objects. The counters in the document are defined to be the same as those counters in the IEEE document, with the intention that the same instrumentation can be used to implement both the IEEE and the IETF management standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects describe a real Ethernet repeater: its ports, its counters, and its address table. The counter definitions are deliberately identical to the ones in the IEEE standard, so one set of measurements can serve both.

sections.title: The Four Packages of Objects
sections.content:
Objects in the MIB are arranged into packages, each containing a set of related objects within a broad functional category. Objects within a package are generally defined under the same OID subtree. The packages are intended for organizational convenience only, and have no relation to the conformance groups defined later in the document.

The basic definitions include objects applicable to all repeaters: status, parameter and control objects for each repeater within the managed system, for the port groups within the system, and for the individual ports themselves. The monitor definitions include monitoring statistics for each repeater within the system and for individual ports. The address tracking definitions include objects for tracking the MAC addresses of the data terminal equipment attached to the ports within the system and for mapping the topology of a network; these are based on a technology which has been patented by Hewlett-Packard, and HP has granted rights to implementors of this MIB to implement it. The Top N definitions may be used for tracking the ports with the most activity within the system or within particular repeaters.

The module sits under mib-2 22, named snmpDot3RptrMgt, with the four packages rooted at 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each package has subtrees for the repeater level, the group level and the port level, and the basic and monitor packages also have a subtree that covers all repeaters in the system at once.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects are sorted into four groups: what a repeater is and what it is doing, how it is counting, where the addresses are, and which ports are busiest. Each group has one subtree per level of the hierarchy: repeater, group of ports, and single port.

sections.title: Why Repeater Ports Are Not Interfaces
sections.content:
It is assumed that a repeater implementing this MIB will also implement, at least, the system group defined in MIB-II. In MIB-II the system group is mandatory for all systems, so that each managed entity contains one instance of each object in the group; those objects therefore apply to the entity even if its sole functionality is the management of repeaters.

The interfaces group in MIB-II is also mandatory for all systems and contains information on an entity's interfaces, where each interface is thought of as being attached to a subnetwork. This Repeater MIB uses the notion of ports on a repeater, and the concept of a MIB-II interface has no specific relationship to a repeater's port. The interfaces group therefore applies only to the one or more network interfaces on which the entity managing the repeater sends and receives management protocol operations, and does not apply to the repeater's ports.

The reasoning is the physical-layer nature of a repeater. A repeater is a bitwise store-and-forward device: it recognises activity and bits, but does not process incoming data based on any packet-related information such as checksums or addresses. A repeater has no MAC address, no MAC implementation, and does not pass packets up to higher-level protocol entities for processing. When a network management entity is observing a repeater, it may appear as though the repeater is passing packets to a higher-level protocol entity, but that is only a means of implementing management, and the passing of management information is not part of the repeater functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: A repeater does not look at packets. It copies signals, so it has no address of its own and it is not a network interface in the MIB-II sense. The management traffic travels over the management entity's own interfaces, not over the repeater's ports.

sections.title: The Managed Objects Themselves
sections.content:
The module defines a table of descriptive and status information about the repeater ports in the system, whose number of entries is independent of the number of repeaters in the managed system. Each entry is indexed by a group index and a port index, and carries the administrative status of the port, with values enabled and disabled; the auto-partition state, with values notAutoPartitioned and autoPartitioned, which indicates whether the port is currently partitioned by the repeater's auto-partition protection, with the conditions that cause partitioning specified in the partition state machine of the IEEE standard and not differentiated here; the operational status; and the identifier of the repeater the port is attached to. The port index identifies the port within the group independently of the repeater it may be attached to, and can never be greater than the port capacity of the associated group.

The monitor package holds the statistics for each repeater and for individual ports. At port level these include readable frames and octets, and the error counters for frame check sequence errors, alignment errors, frames too long, short events, runts, collisions, late events, very long events and data rate mismatches, together with the number of auto-partitions, the total number of errors and the time of the last change. A separate table covers the 100 Mb/s ports.

The address tracking package includes the rptrAddrSearchTable, which contains one entry per repeater in the system and defines objects that allow a management application to instruct an agent to watch for a given MAC address and report which port it was seen on. Only one address search can be in progress on each repeater at any one time, and a management application should obtain ownership of the entry for the repeater that is to perform the search, using the lock, status and owner objects, and the agent increments the lock value when it takes ownership. The address search state reports the outcome, including the group and port where the address was found. A separate search table offers address search across the whole system.

The Top N package contains a table of control records for reports on the top N ports for the rate of a selected counter, where the number of entries depends on the configuration of the agent and the maximum number of entries is implementation dependent. Its objects include the rate base to measure over, the duration and time remaining, the requested and granted size of the report, the start time, the owner, the row status, and the resulting index, group, port and rate for each reported port.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables are the usable part. One lists every port with its status and the repeater it hangs off; one holds the error counters; one lets a manager ask the agent to watch for an address and report the port it appears on; and one asks for a report of the busiest ports over a chosen interval.

sections.title: Mapping the Physical Topology
sections.content:
The network mapping algorithm takes information available from network devices such as repeaters, bridges and switches, and creates a representation of the physical topology of the network.

Networking devices connect to the network through one or more ports, and through those ports the device is capable of hearing network packets sent by other devices. By looking at the source address in a packet, and identifying which port the packet was heard on, the device can tell a network management system where an address is located relative to that device. For bridges and switches the association of address to port can be retrieved from the forwarding database part of the Bridge MIB. For repeaters, the rptrAddrSearchTable may be used to perform the association.

The algorithm then works in steps. It first determines the existence of the network devices and nodes in the network. From that list it selects a starting device, arbitrarily or by some heuristic, and determines where all the other devices are located with respect to it: the starting device sees the others grouped by the port they were heard on, so in the example d1 sees d2 on one port, d3 on another, and d4, d5, d6 and d7 on a third. After that first step the next and final step is recursive: each temporary segment, such as the segment connecting d1 and d2, is examined to determine which of the devices really belongs in that segment, and as new segments are created the recursive algorithm visits them and performs the same process.
sections.plainLanguage: Because each device can say on which port it heard an address, a manager can work out the shape of the network. It starts from one device, groups everything else by the port it was heard on, then repeats the same question inside each group.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document does note, in its description of the address tracking definitions, that those definitions are based on a technology which has been patented by Hewlett-Packard Company, and that HP has granted rights to implementors of this MIB to implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says nothing about security. What it does mention is that the address tracking mechanism comes from a patented technology, and that HP has licensed it to implementors of this MIB.

viz.caption: The four capabilities the new MIB adds

items.title: Multiple repeaters
items.text: One managed system can hold several repeaters, each with its own tables.

items.title: 100BASE-T management
items.text: A separate table covers the 100 Mb/s ports, alongside the 10 Mb/s ones.

items.title: Port TopN capability
items.text: The agent can be asked to report the ports with the highest rate of a chosen counter.

items.title: Address search and topology mapping
items.text: The agent can watch for a MAC address and report the port it was seen on, which is the input to mapping the network.

viz.caption: The four packages under the repeater MIB

cells: An interface of the managed entity, attached to a subnetwork.
A port of a repeater, attached to a segment of the network.
No. A repeater is a bitwise store-and-forward device with no MAC implementation.
Yes, it passes packets up to higher-level protocol entities.
No. It recognises activity and bits, but not checksums or addresses.
On the entity's own network interfaces.
Nowhere. The interfaces group does not apply to the repeater's ports.

items.title: rptrPortGroupIndex
items.text: The group of ports the entry belongs to.

items.title: rptrPortIndex
items.text: The port within the group, identified independently of the repeater it is attached to, and never greater than the group's port capacity.

items.title: rptrPortAdminStatus
items.text: Whether the port is enabled or disabled.

items.title: rptrPortAutoPartitionState
items.text: Whether the port is currently partitioned by the repeater's auto-partition protection.

items.title: rptrPortOperStatus
items.text: Whether the port is working, taking the administrative status and the partition state into account.

items.title: rptrPortRptrId
items.text: The repeater the port is attached to.

viz.caption: The port counters the monitor package keeps

items.title: Readable frames and octets
items.text: The traffic the port passed on.

items.title: Frame check sequence errors
items.text: Frames that arrived with a bad checksum.

items.title: Alignment errors
items.text: Octets that were not octet-aligned.

items.title: Frames too long
items.text: Frames longer than the maximum the port allows.

items.title: Short events, runts and collisions
items.text: The error conditions the IEEE standard defines for a repeater port.

items.title: Late events and very long events
items.text: Collisions that arrive after the frame has finished, and collisions that last unusually long.

items.title: Data rate mismatches
items.text: Frames received at a rate the port cannot handle.

items.title: Auto partitions and total errors
items.text: How often the port has been partitioned automatically, the total error count and the time of the last change.

viz.caption: How the physical map is built

items.title: Find the devices
items.text: Start by determining which devices and nodes exist in the network.

items.title: Pick a starting point
items.text: Choose one device from the list, arbitrarily or by some heuristic.

items.title: Group by port
items.text: Use the address-to-port information to work out which devices the starting device hears on each of its ports.

items.title: Repeat inside each group
items.text: Each temporary segment is examined to see which devices really belong in it, and the algorithm recurses into the segments it creates.
